headline: Thai Rescue Center Doubles Survival Rates for Injured Leopard Cat Cubs
meta_description: A wildlife rescue center in northeastern Thailand has dramatically improved care for injured leopard cat cubs, cutting mortality rates in half through speciali…
summary_short: A Thai rescue center is saving baby leopard cats displaced by habitat loss and agricultural fires, with survival rates jumping from 40% to 67% in recent years.
body:
At a government wildlife rescue center in Khon Kaen, northeastern Thailand, dozens of orphaned and injured leopard cat cubs are getting a second life in the wild. Admissions have surged dramatically—from roughly 10 cats annually to as many as 65 now—driven by habitat fragmentation, agricultural burning in sugarcane fields, and increased awareness among the public, who now report injured animals through a government hotline. The real breakthrough lies in results: mortality rates at the Department of National Parks, Wildlife and Plant Conservation facility have plummeted to around 33 percent in 2026, down from 60 percent in earlier years. More than half of the cubs admitted between January and August arrived from charred fields with burn injuries.

The center's success hinges on rigorous protocols. Veterinarians like Warisara Thomas stabilize arrivals by treating burns and infections, then move healthy cubs into specialized 24-square-meter enclosures for two-month rehabilitation programs. The cats learn to hunt live prey—mice and chicks—to build survival instincts while gradually learning to distrust humans. Before release, each cub receives health screening for serious viruses and is microchipped for identification. This careful preparation mirrors what conservation experts call a "soft release," which Jim Sanderson of the Small Wild Cat Conservation Foundation describes as "absolutely vital" for rehabilitated wild cats.

Once cleared, the cubs are released into nearby Phu Pha Man National Park. Yet success brings new challenges: local protected forests are reaching capacity, prompting center officials to explore additional release sites. The work underscores a broader truth—sometimes saving endangered wildlife means rescuing them one cub at a time, with patience, science, and a second chance.
quick_facts: Admissions jumped from 10 to 65 leopard cat cubs annually at Thai rescue center
More than half of recent arrivals had burn injuries from agricultural fires
Survival rates improved to 67% from 40% through specialized rehabilitation care
Each cub undergoes two-month training program before release to wild
Located at Department of National Parks facility in Khon Kaen, northeastern Thailand
